entries:
From Middle High German hornunc, from Old High German hornung (“bastard”) (viz.); one of Charlemagne's proposed names for reformed calendar months with limited success, according to Einhard.
The apparent semantic connection has been postulated to February being the "odd one out" amongst months (shortest and changing dates), hence the "bastard month".
Compare Pennsylvania German Hanning, Old English hornungsunu (“bastard”), Frankish hōrni(n)g.

entries:
Zukunft + -s- + Musik, “music of the future”. Initially coined as term of abuse for Richard Wagner's music by Ludwig Bischoff in the 1850s., the original sense being "music that will only find appreciation in the future".
As a metaphor for non-musical plans and ideas, it occurs as early as the 1890s.
